slides.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
slides.subtitle: The staircase, the air, the water in your bottle, the food in your lunch box — almost nothing around you is made of just one substance.
points: Which of the things around you consist of matter, and which do not?
How can simple elements be combined to form a compound?
How could the discovery of a compound that absorbs carbon dioxide help solve environmental challenges?

slides.title: What are mixtures?
slides.intro: What makes your poha so delicious, or a sprout salad so colourful? Both are made by mixing several ingredients. Let's see what happens when substances come together.

slides.title: Substances mixed, but unchanged
slides.body: When two or more substances are mixed and each one **keeps its own properties**, the result is a **mixture**. The individual substances that make it up are its **components**, and they do **not react chemically** with each other. Poha, sprout salad, sugar in water, soups, and lemonade are all mixtures.

slides.title: Non-uniform and uniform mixtures
slides.leftBody: Components are clearly visible to the naked eye or a magnifying glass — like the green gram, chickpeas, onion, and tomato in a sprout salad.
slides.rightBody: Components are evenly distributed and cannot be told apart even under a microscope — like sugar and water particles in a glass of sugar water.

slides.title: Alloys are mixtures too
slides.body: Stainless steel is a mixture of **iron, nickel, chromium**, and a little carbon, blended so uniformly you cannot see the separate metals. Such mixtures are called **alloys**. **Brass** (copper and zinc) and **bronze** (copper and tin) are other examples.

slides.translation: Ancient Indian texts such as the Charaka Samhita, Susruta Samhita, and Rasa Jala Nidhi describe alloys with properties distinct from their parent metals. Bronze, or Kamsya — Copper (Tamra, 4 parts) and Tin (Vanga, 1 part) — was used to improve digestion and boost immunity.

slides.title: Is air a mixture?
slides.intro: You learnt about air and its composition back in Grade 6. So — is air a mixture, and what kind?

slides.title: Air is a uniform mixture
slides.body: Air is a **uniform mixture** of mainly **nitrogen** (about 78%), **oxygen**, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. Oxygen keeps living beings alive and supports combustion; nitrogen does not take part in combustion. Air also carries water vapour, which forms tiny droplets when warm air meets a cool surface.

slides.title: Confirm the carbon dioxide in air
slides.purpose: We exhale carbon dioxide — but is it also present in ordinary air? We make lime water and leave it open to the air to find out. (Handle the calcium oxide carefully — it reacts vigorously.)
steps: Make — add a little calcium oxide (quick lime) to half a tumbler of water; it heats up and forms calcium hydroxide
Filter — stir, filter, and pour the clear colourless lime water into a petri dish
Wait — leave it for a few hours, stirring at intervals, and watch
slides.observe: The lime water slowly **turns milky**. Carbon dioxide from the air reacts with calcium hydroxide to form **calcium carbonate** (insoluble white particles) and water — proving carbon dioxide is present in the air: Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water.

slides.title: Catch what floats in the air
slides.purpose: Apart from gases, is anything else present in air? We leave a clean black sheet exposed to see what settles on it.
steps: Prepare — take a black sheet of paper, free of any visible dust
Expose — leave it undisturbed near an open window or in the garden for a few hours
Examine — look at its surface, then more closely with a magnifying glass
slides.observe: Tiny **dust particles** settle on the sheet — they are **suspended in the air** and counted as pollutants. The number and nature of dust particles vary from place to place and time to time; the **air quality index (AQI)** describes how clean or polluted the air is.

slides.title: Types of mixtures
slides.intro: Mixtures come in several types depending on the physical state of their components. In science, all the components of a mixture must themselves be pure substances.

slides.title: Mixtures by the state of their parts
What are pure substances?
slides.intro: You've seen 'pure' printed on packs of milk, ghee, and spices. But 'pure' means something slightly different in everyday speech and in science.

slides.title: Pure means just one substance
slides.body: In everyday use, **pure** means unadulterated — free of cheaper or poor-quality additives. **Adulteration** is the illegal mixing-in of such substances to cut cost. In science, a **pure substance** has only **one kind of particle** and cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any **physical process**. By that test, even milk and packed juice count as mixtures.

slides.title: What are the types of pure substances?
slides.intro: Cooling and heating only change water between ice, liquid, and vapour — the particles stay the same. But what happens when we pass electricity through water?

slides.title: Pass electricity through water
slides.purpose: Cooling or boiling never changes what water is made of. We pass an electric current through it to test whether water can be split into something simpler. (Do this only with a teacher; handle dilute sulfuric acid with care, and never use a lithium-ion battery.)
steps: Set up — fill a beaker with water, add a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid, and stand a 9 V battery inside it
Invert — fill two test tubes with the same water and place one over each terminal of the battery
Wait — let it run for 10–15 minutes and watch the gas bubbles collect at both terminals
Test — bring a burning candle to the mouth of each tube
slides.observe: Gas collects in **both** tubes — about **twice as much over one terminal** as the other. One gives a **'pop' sound** (hydrogen), and the other makes the **flame glow brighter** (oxygen). So water is made of two different constituents: Water → Hydrogen + Oxygen.

slides.title: Elements
slides.intro: The hydrogen and oxygen released from water cannot be broken down any further. What do we call such substances?

slides.title: Elements cannot be broken down
slides.body: Hydrogen and oxygen are **elements** — pure substances that **cannot be broken down** into anything simpler. Each element is made of identical particles called **atoms**, different from the atoms of every other element. Elements are the building blocks of all matter. Gold, silver, sulfur, and carbon are other examples.

slides.title: When atoms join into molecules
slides.body: The atoms of most elements **cannot exist on their own**. Two or more such atoms combine into a stable particle called a **molecule**. Two hydrogen atoms join to form one molecule of hydrogen, and two oxygen atoms form one molecule of oxygen.

slides.title: Metals and non-metals
slides.leftBody: Gold, silver, magnesium, iron, and aluminium. Of all 118 known elements, most exist as solids — only mercury (a metal) is liquid at room temperature.
slides.rightBody: Carbon, sulfur, hydrogen, and oxygen. Eleven elements are gases at room temperature. Silicon and boron have in-between properties and are called metalloids.

slides.title: Compounds
slides.intro: Why can't we separate the hydrogen and oxygen in water by physical means? Because in water they are bound together as a compound.

slides.title: A compound is something entirely new
slides.body: A **compound** forms when different elements combine **chemically in a fixed ratio**, and it **cannot be separated by any physical method**. In water, hydrogen and oxygen atoms are bound in a fixed **2:1 ratio**. Its properties are **entirely different** from its elements: hydrogen is a fuel and oxygen supports combustion, yet water puts out fire.

slides.title: Common salt: when metal meets gas
slides.body: **Sodium**, a soft metal, and **chlorine**, a hazardous gas, combine in a **1:1 ratio** to form harmless, taste-enhancing **sodium chloride** — common salt. Dissolved salt can be recovered from water by evaporation (a physical change), but salt itself cannot be split into sodium and chlorine by any physical process.

slides.title: Heat sugar and see what's left
slides.purpose: Is sugar an element or a compound? We heat it gently and watch what it breaks into. (Do this in the presence of a teacher.)
steps: Heat — put a teaspoon of sugar in a boiling tube and warm it gently
Watch — the colour change as it heats
Collect — scoop out what remains onto a watch glass
slides.observe: The sugar turns **brown, then black (chars)**, droplets of **water** appear near the tube's mouth, and **charcoal (carbon)** is left behind. So sugar is a **compound** of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen — it cannot be an element.

slides.title: Iron and sulfur: mixture vs compound
slides.purpose: Mixing two elements, then heating them, shows the difference between a mixture and a compound. We compare the two side by side. (Demonstrate under a teacher, in a well-ventilated area; do not inhale the gases.)
steps: Mix — combine 5.6 g iron filings with 3.2 g sulfur powder on a watch glass; call this Sample A
Heat — heat half of Sample A with stirring until a black mass forms; grind it and call it Sample B
Test — compare A and B by appearance, a magnet, and a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid
slides.observe: **Sample A** is a **mixture**: you still see black and yellow specks, the magnet pulls the iron out, and acid gives odourless hydrogen (a 'pop'). **Sample B** is **iron sulfide**, a **compound**: uniform black, not attracted by the magnet, and acid releases foul, rotten-egg-smelling **hydrogen sulfide**. Its properties are completely new, and iron and sulfur can no longer be separated.

slides.title: Element, compound, and mixture
slides.caption: An element is identical atoms; a compound is different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio; a mixture is different particles, unbonded and separable.

slides.title: How do we use elements, compounds, and mixtures?
slides.intro: These three kinds of matter are all around us — and understanding them is the key to innovation.

slides.title: From bridges to medicines
slides.body: The **air** we breathe is a mixture of gases; **water** is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen; **iron** and **aluminium** are elements used to build bridges, buildings, and vehicles. Chemists combine elements to invent **medicines, vaccines, and fertilisers**, and engineers design **alloys** like stainless steel — stronger and more durable than pure iron.

slides.title: What are minerals?
slides.intro: Various metals are obtained from minerals. Most rocks are themselves mixtures of minerals. Let's take a closer look.

slides.title: Most minerals are compounds
slides.body: Most rocks are **mixtures of minerals**. A few are **native minerals** — pure elements, not compounds — such as gold, silver, copper, sulfur, or carbon. But **most minerals are compounds** of more than one element, like quartz, calcite, mica, pyroxene, and olivine. Cement comes from calcite and quartz; talcum powder from the mineral **talc**.

slides.transliteration: Dhokra — metal-casting art of Bihar and Odisha
slides.translation: A design is first shaped in beeswax, covered in clay to form a mould, and the wax is melted out. The hollow is filled with molten brass or bronze, which makes Dhokra art strong and gives it a shiny golden colour — figures of animals, people, and nature reflecting tribal creativity.

slides.title: What is matter — and what isn't
slides.body: Elements and compounds are the **building blocks of matter** — everything that has **mass and takes up space**. But not everything around us is matter. **Light, heat, electricity**, and even thoughts and emotions are important parts of our world, yet they are **not made of matter**.

slides.title: Elements, compounds, mixtures — sorted
slides.subtitle: From the air you breathe to the salt on your plate, the water in your bottle, and the alloys of Mishraloha, you can now read the world as the matter it's made of.
